# Quit Smoking Hub Data Center — full content
<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/behavior-change/index.md -->

# Behaviour Change: The Mechanisms

Quitting is a behaviour change problem layered on a pharmacological one. This section covers the behavioural science concepts the platform uses.

## Cue → routine → reward

Most smoking is habitual: a **cue** (coffee, alcohol, stress, driving) triggers a **routine** (lighting up) that delivers a **reward** (nicotine spike + ritual relief). After quitting, the cues remain for months — which is why cravings return in old contexts. The standard strategy is to keep the cue, change the routine, and substitute a reward.

## Lapse vs relapse — the core distinction

| | Lapse | Relapse |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | A single slip: one or a few cigarettes | Return to regular smoking |
| What it means | The quit attempt is damaged, not ended | The quit attempt has ended |
| Correct response | Analyze the trigger, renew the plan, continue quitting | Start a new quit attempt — attempt count is not failure |

The evidence does not support treating a lapse as catastrophic. People who respond to a slip by recommitting are common among successful long-term quitters — see [Relapse section](../relapse/).

## Self-efficacy

Belief in one's ability to quit predicts success in the literature. Self-efficacy is built by surviving high-risk situations without smoking — each survived trigger makes the next one easier. This is why lapse management ("what will I do differently next time") matters more than self-blame.

## Implementation intentions

"If-then" planning ("if I want a cigarette after dinner, then I will brush my teeth immediately") consistently outperforms vague intentions in behaviour-change research. The [main site tools page](https://smokingcessationhub.com/tools/) provides practical versions.

## Why willpower framing is incomplete

Quitting framed purely as "willpower" ignores pharmacology (dependence is neurobiological), conditioning (cues fire automatically), and environment (access and social context). The evidence-based framing is: reduce biological demand (medication), reprogramme cues (behaviour change), and change the environment (removing cigarettes, managing triggers). None of these is about moral strength.

## Related

- [Relapse section](../relapse/) — lapse, relapse and recovery in the evidence
- [Community patterns](https://smokingcessationhub.com/patterns/) — patterns observed across community experiences (main site)

# Cessation Methods: The Evidence

How the evidence compares across the main ways people quit. This page is the evidence layer; the practical comparison lives on the [main site methods section](https://smokingcessationhub.com/methods/).

## Evidence strength by method

| Method | Best available evidence | Direction of findings |
|---|---|---|
| Varenicline | Cochrane partial-agonists review (R-002); EAGLES (R-015) | Most effective single medication in network analyses |
| NRT (patch + fast-acting) | Cochrane NRT review (R-001) | ~50–70% increase in quit rates vs placebo |
| Cytisine | West 2011 (R-016); Walker 2014 (R-017) | Superior to placebo; comparable to NRT at lower cost |
| Bupropion | Cochrane antidepressant review (R-003) | Roughly doubles quit rates vs placebo |
| Combination NRT | Cochrane overview (R-008) | Patch + fast-acting form more effective than one form |
| Counselling / behavioural support | USPSTF 2021; WHO 2024 | Effective alone; more effective combined with medication |
| Quitlines | WHO 2024; US PHS 2008 | Effective population-level support |
| Digital interventions | WHO 2024 | Recommended as complement; evidence base growing |
| Peer support | Community-level; mixed formal evidence | Real-world valued; formal trial evidence limited |
| Cold turkey (unaided) | Observational data | Most common in the community (see community statistics), lower per-attempt success than aided quitting in trial literature |
| Gradual reduction | Cochrane R-004 | Abrupt and gradual produce similar quit rates when supported; evidence on reduction alone is weaker |

## Three reading rules

1. **"Effective" is statistical, not personal.** A method that helps more people on average may not be the right one for a given individual.
2. **Combination beats monotherapy.** Medication + behavioural support is the single most consistent finding across guidelines.
3. **Community popularity ≠ evidence strength.** Cold turkey dominates community reports but is not the most effective aided approach in trials. Both facts can be true — see [Community Data](../community-data/statistics.md).

## Related

- [Medications](../medications/) — per-medication evidence pages
- [Research Database](../research/) — the underlying records
- [Controversies](../controversies/) — where the evidence genuinely conflicts

# Community Data Center

This section of the Data Center documents the **structured community experience database** that powers the experiential layer of Quit Smoking Hub. It describes where the data comes from, how it is processed, what rules protect privacy and safety, and what the aggregate statistics currently show.

## What this dataset is

The community experience database is a collection of structured, de-identified records synthesized from real quit-smoking experiences shared in a large public Chinese-language quit-smoking forum (Baidu Tieba's 戒烟吧 / "Quit Smoking Bar"). The forum has operated for nearly two decades and contains tens of thousands of first-person quit accounts, check-in diaries, relapse reports and Q&A threads.

Each record captures, where the source reports it:

- smoking history (years, cigarettes per day, age group)
- quit method(s) used
- recovery stage and day count
- triggers and cravings
- physical symptoms and emotional state
- strategies and interventions
- outcome and relapse information
- lessons the person drew

## What this dataset is not

!!! warning "Community reports are not scientific evidence"
    Every record is a **community report** — one person's account of their own experience, as posted in a public forum. The records:

    - are **not** clinical data and were not medically verified;
    - are **not** a substitute for research findings, guidelines, or medical advice;
    - may contain selection bias: people who post in a quit-smoking forum are a specific subset of all people who try to quit;
    - cannot support causal claims about any method, symptom, or medication.

    Aggregate statistics below describe *what this forum's members reported*, nothing more.

## Privacy and ethics rules

The ingestion pipeline follows these rules, which are enforced for every record:

1. **No usernames, user IDs, avatars, or contact information** are ever stored or published.
2. **No verbatim copying or wholesale translation** of any post — records are original English editorial syntheses of the reported facts.
3. **Unreported fields are marked "Not reported"** — nothing is inferred to fill gaps.
4. **Thin records** (insufficient information) remain in the internal database and are marked `noindex`; they generate no public pages.
5. **Medical safety gate**: content indicating mental-health high risk (e.g. self-harm, crisis) is held in `review` status and never auto-published.
6. **Non-judgmental language**: the site uses "relapse" and "return to smoking", never "failure" or "weakness".

## Where the records live

The full structured records are maintained in the main site's content repository ([SmokingCessation](https://github.com/martinxionbiotech-max/SmokingCessation), `src/data/experiences/`, `src/data/relapse/`, `src/data/patterns/`). Public pages render at:

- [Community Experiences](https://smokingcessationhub.com/experiences/) — individual experience pages
- [Relapse Reports](https://smokingcessationhub.com/relapse/) — structured relapse records
- [Community Patterns](https://smokingcessationhub.com/patterns/) — patterns observed across multiple reports

See also the ingestion pipeline documentation ([CONTENT-INGESTION.md](https://github.com/martinxionbiotech-max/SmokingCessation/blob/main/CONTENT-INGESTION.md)) and the data model ([DATA-MODEL.md](https://github.com/martinxionbiotech-max/SmokingCessation/blob/main/DATA-MODEL.md)).

## Current statistics

[View the live aggregate statistics](statistics.md), recomputed from the record database after each ingestion batch.


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/community-data/statistics.md -->

# Community Data — Live Statistics

*Computed from the structured record database on 2026-10-04 (after ingestion batch 7). Figures describe de-identified reports from one public quit-smoking forum — they are not clinical data and not generalizable to all quitters.*

## Database size

| Record type | Count |
|---|---|
| Experience records (total) | **169** |
| — published (public pages) | 133 |
| — noindex (internal database only) | 34 |
| — review (medical safety gate) | 2 |
| Relapse reports | 12 |
| Community patterns | 6 |
| Questions | 12 |

## Quality distribution (published experiences)

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean quality score | 7.3 / 10 |
| Minimum (publish threshold) | 6 / 10 |
| Maximum | 9 / 10 |

Quality scoring follows the rubric in [CONTENT-QUALITY.md](https://github.com/martinxionbiotech-max/SmokingCessation/blob/main/CONTENT-QUALITY.md): information density, specificity, honesty about unknowns, and evidence labeling.

## Quit methods reported

Across 133 published experience records (a record may report more than one method):

| Method | Records |
|---|---|
| Cold turkey | 29 |
| Reading-based program (Allen Carr) | 7 |
| Daily community check-ins | 4 |
| Gradual reduction | 3 |
| Exercise | 2 |
| Diet change | 2 |
| Smoking cessation medication (type unspecified) | 1 |
| Removing all smoking devices | 1 |
| Quitting alcohol at the same time | 1 |
| E-cigarette substitution | 1 |
| Nicotine replacement (patch) | 1 |

## Smoking history reported

- 70 of 133 published records (53%) report years of smoking; the rest are marked "Not reported".
- Reported histories range from 3 to 40 years; 39 records fall in the 10–20 year range and 25 in the 21–40 year range.
- Age groups reported: 20s (7), 30s (7), 40s (3), 50s (1) — most records do not state age.
- Gender reported: female (2) — most records do not state gender.

## Relapse

- 13 of 133 published experience records (10%) describe at least one previous relapse.
- The 12 structured relapse reports record time smoke-free before relapse:

| Time smoke-free before relapse | Reports |
|---|---|
| 2–3 months | 5 |
| 100 days | 1 |
| 6 months | 1 |
| 7 months | 2 |
| 9 months | 1 |
| 1 year | 1 |
| 1.5 years | 1 |
| ~4 years | 1 |

One structured report spans two relapses (6 months, then 3 months) and appears in both rows. Beyond the structured reports, one published experience (EXP-2020-005) records a quit of roughly 1,730 days — nearly five years — that was lost, followed by a new attempt: the longest relapse-free period documented in the database.

### Patterns observed across reports

1. **Alcohol and social occasions** — the most reported relapse setting (6 relevant reports), including one report of surviving drinking situations smoke-free (a contradictory case).
2. **Relapse returns a heavier habit** — several reports describe smoking more after relapse than before the quit (3 relevant reports).
3. **The first cigarette is the relapse** — a single cigarette taken as reward or accepted casually was the pivot point of relapse in multiple reports (6 relevant reports), including two near-miss cases in which the slip was contained and the quit continued.
4. **Smoking dreams** — vivid dreams about smoking, usually arriving around a month into the quit and treated by reporters as a passing phase rather than a warning (3 relevant reports; none relapsed).
5. **Health events as the decisive motivation** — quits started from a hospitalization, diagnosis, a relative's smoking-related death or alarming test results, described as feeling different from gradual decisions (9 relevant reports).
6. **Daily check-ins as a commitment device** — daily sign-in rituals maintained for years, in two cases a decade, with the streak and its public visibility anchoring the quit (6 relevant reports).

## Most-reported symptoms (published records)

Symptoms are self-reported withdrawal or health effects, not diagnoses:

| Symptom | Records |
|---|---|
| Chest tightness | 6 |
| Dizziness | 5 |
| Irritability | 4 |
| Shortness of breath | 4 |
| Cough | 3 |
| Phlegm | 3 |
| Blurred vision | 2 |
| Weakness | 2 |
| Anxiety | 2 |
| Drowsiness | 2 |
| Stomach bloating | 2 |
| Insomnia | 2 |
| Poor concentration | 2 |

## Recovery stages represented

| Stage | Records |
|---|---|
| First Week | 22 |
| Long-Term | 18 |
| First Month | 7 |
| First Three Weeks | 6 |
| First Two Months | 4 |
| First Two Weeks | 4 |
| First Three Months | 4 |
| Week 3 | 3 |
| Other stages (2 weeks – 1 year) | 3 |

## Evidence status

Every record in the database is labeled `community-report` (169 of 169). The evidence-status scale (`community-report` → `pattern-supported` → `evidence-aligned` → `evidence-mixed`) is applied when patterns and research alignment are assessed; currently the `pattern-supported` level is in use on the six pattern pages.

## How these numbers change

Statistics are recomputed after each ingestion batch. Each batch:

1. collects source material only from real, public forum posts;
2. applies the privacy filter and de-identification rules;
3. structures records against the published data model;
4. deduplicates against existing records;
5. writes an original English editorial synthesis (no verbatim translation);
6. assigns quality score, confidence level, and editorial status (`published` / `noindex` / `review`);
7. rebuilds the site — noindex and review records never produce public pages.


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/controversies/dual-use.md -->

# Dual Use: Smoking + Vaping

Using e-cigarettes while still smoking cigarettes. Positioned by some as a transition stage; by others as a trap.

## Evidence supporting dual use as a bridge

- In observational data, some dual users later transition to exclusive vaping or quit entirely; vaping reduces cigarette consumption for some.
- Harm-reduction logic: fewer cigarettes smoked means lower (not zero) toxicant exposure, and NRT harm-reduction precedents exist.

## Evidence against / limitations

- **Most dual users remain dual users** — in several cohort studies the majority do not quit smoking within follow-up.
- Continued smoking keeps most smoking-related risk; harm reduction requires actually stopping cigarettes.
- Nicotine intake can be higher during dual use than while smoking alone, prolonging dependence.
- WHO cautions that dual use can sustain smoking rather than end it.

## What is known vs uncertain

- **Known**: dual use reduces harm only insofar as it reduces cigarette consumption; it does not eliminate smoking risk; many dual users do not transition.
- **Uncertain**: how often dual use is a genuine stepping stone versus a lasting state; long-term outcomes.

## Platform treatment

Community records that describe dual use are reported as experiences. The platform's position: **the goal is stopping combustible cigarettes**; dual use is at best an unstable intermediate state, and anyone dual-using is encouraged to set a date to stop cigarettes completely.


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/controversies/e-cigarettes.md -->

# E-Cigarettes for Smoking Cessation

The single largest controversy in cessation. The evidence is strong in one direction and the guidelines genuinely split.

## Evidence supporting e-cigarettes as cessation aids

- **Cochrane living review (2024 update, R-013)**: high-certainty evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes increase quit rates compared with NRT; moderate-certainty evidence versus behavioural support or no support. This upgraded earlier (moderate) certainty ratings.
- **Hajek et al., NEJM 2019 (R-005)**: in a UK stop-smoking service, e-cigarette users achieved roughly double the 1-year abstinence of NRT users (18.0% vs 9.9%).
- **NICE NG209**: clinicians may offer nicotine-containing e-cigarettes to people interested in using them to quit, with advice to stop smoking completely.

## Evidence against / limitations

- **Long-term safety is unknown.** E-cigarettes are a relatively new product class; decades-long outcomes do not exist. Non-nicotine constituents (flavourings, aerosol byproducts) are under active study.
- **WHO (2024)**: does not recommend e-cigarettes as cessation aids, citing insufficient evidence of safety and effectiveness at population level; notes industry involvement in the market.
- **USPSTF (2021)**: I statement — evidence insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms; directs clinicians to interventions with proven effectiveness.
- **Youth uptake concern**: non-smoking young people who vape are at higher risk of later cigarette smoking in observational studies — a public-health harm independent of any cessation benefit.
- **Dual use** is common and its net effect is debated (see [dual-use](dual-use.md)).

## Guideline positions (as published)

| Body | Position |
|---|---|
| Cochrane (evidence body) | High-certainty evidence of efficacy vs NRT |
| NICE NG209 (UK) | May be offered as a cessation aid |
| WHO 2024 | Not recommended as cessation aid |
| USPSTF 2021 (US) | Evidence insufficient (I) |

## What is known vs uncertain

- **Known**: nicotine e-cigarettes outperform NRT in randomized trials for quitting; they are not harmless; they are inappropriate for non-smokers, especially youth.
- **Uncertain**: long-term health effects; net population impact; optimal role relative to approved medications.

## Platform position

The platform treats e-cigarettes as **experimental-adjacent but trial-supported** — stronger than "unproven", weaker than approved medications, and never for non-smokers. Community reports of vaping-assisted quits are recorded in the experience database without endorsement.


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/controversies/gradual-vs-abrupt.md -->

# Gradual Reduction vs Abrupt Quitting

A public debate with a surprisingly clear evidence picture — and a notable community-vs-trial divergence.

## What the evidence says

- **Cochrane R-004** (Lindson-Hawley et al.): among people who want to quit, quitting abruptly and quitting by gradual reduction **with support** produce similar long-term quit rates. Gradual reduction without any support is less well evidenced.
- **NICE NG209** supports staged reduction with temporary use of licensed nicotine products for people not ready to stop in one go.
- The old folk belief that "cutting down first weakens the attempt" is not supported by the trial literature.

## Why the debate persists

- **Community experience skews cold turkey.** In the platform's own experience database, cold turkey is by far the most reported method (see [community statistics](../community-data/statistics.md)), and many long-term quitters credit the clean break.
- **Selection effect**: people who choose cold turkey may differ from those who choose reduction (motivation, dependence, support). Observational popularity does not prove comparative effectiveness.
- **"Gradual" means different things**: self-managed cutting-down versus supported reduction with NRT are different interventions with different evidence.

## What this means practically

Both routes are legitimate. The evidence-backed advice is: whichever route, **set a fixed quit date and use the strongest support available** — the difference between methods is smaller than the difference between supported and unsupported attempts.

## Positions

- Trial literature: no meaningful difference when both are supported.
- Community experience: strong preference for abrupt, often credited with success.
- Platform: presents both, treats the community preference as a reported pattern, not proof of superiority.


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/controversies/index.md -->

# Controversies

Topics where the published evidence genuinely conflicts, is contested, or remains insufficient. This section presents positions as they are actually held — by named guidelines and studies — without taking sides. Controversies are not manufactured: each topic here has real divergence in the literature or among major guideline bodies.

## Current topics

1. **[E-cigarettes for smoking cessation](e-cigarettes.md)** — Cochrane finds high-certainty evidence they help people quit; WHO and USPSTF decline to recommend them; NICE explicitly allows offering them. Long-term safety unknown.
2. **[Gradual reduction vs abrupt quitting](gradual-vs-abrupt.md)** — the Cochrane evidence says supported gradual and abrupt quitting produce similar quit rates; community experience strongly favors cold turkey; the public debate persists.
3. **[Dual use (smoking + vaping)](dual-use.md)** — is it a bridge to quitting or a trap that sustains smoking?
4. **[Medication comparisons](medication-comparisons.md)** — varenicline vs cytisine vs NRT combinations: what the network meta-analyses actually say.

## Reading rules for this section

- Every position is attributed and dated.
- "Evidence supporting" and "evidence against / limitations" are listed separately.
- Where guidelines disagree, the disagreement is stated flatly — the platform does not arbitrate.
- This is not a list of "both sides" of settled questions. Settled questions (e.g., whether smoking causes cancer) are not controversies.


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/controversies/medication-comparisons.md -->

# Medication Comparisons: What the Network Meta-Analyses Say

The comparative evidence on cessation medications, from the Cochrane network meta-analysis tradition.

## The main comparisons

- **Varenicline vs NRT monotherapy**: varenicline generally emerges as the more effective single agent in network meta-analyses (R-008; Cochrane partial-agonists review R-002).
- **Varenicline vs bupropion**: varenicline generally superior on quit rates (R-002, R-008).
- **Cytisine vs NRT**: Walker 2014 (R-017) found cytisine noninferior-to-superior at 1 month, with the difference narrowing and becoming non-significant at 6 months — at much lower cost. Cochrane partial-agonists analyses include cytisine (R-002).
- **Cytisine vs varenicline**: fewer head-to-head trials; both are partial agonists; varenicline has the larger trial base.
- **Combination NRT** (patch + fast-acting form): more effective than single-form NRT (R-008) — the standard advice in UK services.
- **E-cigarettes vs NRT**: high-certainty evidence favors nicotine e-cigarettes (R-013) — but see the [e-cigarettes controversy](e-cigarettes.md) for the full picture.

## What is genuinely uncertain

- Whether cytisine fully matches varenicline in direct comparison (ongoing trials).
- Optimal duration of treatment.
- Which medication is best for specific subgroups (heavy smokers, psychiatric comorbidity, pregnancy — USPSTF marks pregnancy pharmacotherapy as an I statement).

## Reading note

"More effective on average" is not "better for you". Choice involves cost, availability, side-effect profile, prior experience and preference — which is why every medication page here ends with questions for a healthcare professional, and why this platform never ranks medications for individuals.

## Related records

- [R-002](../research/records/r-002.md) · [R-008](../research/records/r-008.md) · [R-013](../research/records/r-013.md) · [R-017](../research/records/r-017.md)


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/definitions/index.md -->

# Definitions

The glossary of defined terms used across this platform. Each definition is written to be clear, stable, and consistent between the main site and the data site. Where a term has a formal technical meaning, the plain-language version is given first.

## Core terms

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Abstinence** | Sustained non-smoking over a defined period (e.g., continuous abstinence since a quit date). |
| **Craving** | An intense urge to smoke; has a pharmacological component (nicotine-adapted brain) and a conditioned component (triggers). |
| **Trigger** | A cue — internal (stress, alcohol, boredom) or external (coffee, driving, social events) — that activates the urge to smoke. |
| **Withdrawal** | The symptom syndrome that follows nicotine removal as the brain and body re-adapt; peaks in week 1, mostly resolves in 2–4 weeks. |
| **Lapse** | A single slip — one or a few cigarettes after a quit date. Not the end of the quit attempt. |
| **Relapse** | Return to regular, ongoing smoking; the quit attempt has ended. |
| **Quit attempt** | A deliberate, dated attempt to stop smoking, regardless of outcome. |
| **Quit date** | The planned day smoking stops. |
| **Nicotine dependence** | Neuroadaptation to nicotine producing craving, tolerance and withdrawal on removal. |
| **NRT** | Nicotine replacement therapy: patch, gum, lozenge, inhaler or spray delivering nicotine without tobacco smoke. |
| **Cold turkey** | Stopping smoking abruptly, without medication or gradual reduction. |
| **Gradual reduction** | Tapering cigarette consumption before a quit date, with or without nicotine products. |
| **Harm reduction** | Strategies to reduce harm without full abstinence (e.g., switching to lower-risk nicotine products); distinct from cessation. |
| **Dual use** | Using e-cigarettes or other products while still smoking cigarettes. |
| **Evidence strength** | Grading of a research record: Strong / Moderate / Limited, based on design and consistency. |

## Evidence vocabulary used on this platform

| Phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Evidence says…** | Statement supported by published research at evidence levels 1–5 (see [Research](../research/)). |
| **Community reports…** | Observation drawn from the de-identified experience database — not medical evidence. |
| **What remains uncertain…** | Genuine gaps or conflicts in the published evidence. |

## Related

- [Research Database](../research/) — where evidence strength is applied
- [Main site methodology](https://smokingcessationhub.com/methodology/) — how community data is collected and graded


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/guidelines/index.md -->

# Clinical & Public Health Guidelines

Structured comparison of authoritative cessation guidelines. Every entry records the issuing body, year, scope, key recommendations and where the guidelines differ. Sources are Tier-1: WHO, national health agencies and independent guideline bodies.

**Rule:** guideline positions are reported as published, with the guideline date stated. Positions are never paraphrased into stronger or weaker claims than the source makes.

## Guideline comparison at a glance

| Body | Document | Year | Pharmacotherapy position | Behavioural support | E-cigarettes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| WHO | Clinical treatment guideline for tobacco cessation in adults | 2024 | Recommends varenicline, NRT, bupropion, cytisine | Strongly recommended (brief advice + intensive support) | No recommendation for cessation use; evidence insufficient |
| USPSTF (US) | Tobacco Smoking Cessation in Adults, Including Pregnant Persons | 2021 | Recommends FDA-approved pharmacotherapy for nonpregnant adults (A) | Recommends behavioural interventions (A) | Evidence insufficient (I statement) |
| NICE (UK) | NG209 Tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting and treating dependence | 2021 (last reviewed 2025) | Recommends varenicline, NRT, bupropion, cytisine options | Behavioural support for all, intensively for some | Nicotine-containing e-cigarettes can be offered as an aid |
| US PHS | Treating Tobacco Use and Dependence: 2008 Update | 2008 | First-line: 7 approved medications | Counseling + medication combined recommended | Predates modern evidence base |

## Records

- [WHO 2024 — clinical treatment guideline](who-2024.md)
- [USPSTF 2021 — recommendation statement](uspstf-2021.md)
- [NICE NG209 — tobacco dependence guideline](nice-ng209.md)
- [US PHS 2008 — Treating Tobacco Use and Dependence](usphs-2008.md)

## How to read these records

Guidelines are statements by specific bodies at specific dates. They can and do differ — on e-cigarettes, on medication ordering, and on how strongly behavioural support is emphasized. Differences usually reflect different evidence cut-off dates, different regulatory contexts and different risk tolerances, not scientific disagreement about core facts. Where positions differ, this site states the difference rather than picking a winner.


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/guidelines/nice-ng209.md -->

# NICE NG209 — Tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting and treating dependence

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Issuing body | National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (UK) |
| Year | 2021; last reviewed 4 February 2025 |
| Scope | Support to stop smoking for everyone aged 12 and over; harm reduction; prevention of uptake in children, young people and young adults (up to 24) |
| Source | [nice.org.uk/guidance/ng209](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng209) |

## Key positions

- **Behavioural support**: individual or group behavioural support should be offered to everyone who wants to quit; it should not be rationed by "readiness to quit".
- **Medications**: varenicline and NRT (alone or combined) are the principal options; bupropion and cytisine are also covered — the 2025 review added new recommendations on cytisinicline (cytisine).
- **E-cigarettes**: clinicians can offer nicotine-containing e-cigarettes as an aid for people interested in using them to quit smoking; users should be advised to stop smoking completely.
- **Harm reduction**: for people not ready to stop in one go, supports staged reduction, including temporary use of licensed nicotine products.

## Notable differences

NG209 is the most e-cigarette-accommodating of the major guidelines: it treats nicotine-containing e-cigarettes as a legitimate offer, in contrast to WHO (insufficient evidence) and USPSTF (I statement). NG209 also explicitly addresses harm reduction and gradual approaches, and extends to people aged 12 and over.


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/guidelines/usphs-2008.md -->

# US PHS 2008 — Treating Tobacco Use and Dependence: 2008 Update

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Issuing body | US Public Health Service (Clinical Practice Guideline) |
| Year | 2008 (updated from 2000) |
| Scope | Clinical treatment of tobacco dependence in adults |
| Source | Treating Tobacco Use and Dependence: 2008 Update (AHRQ) |

## Key positions (as published in 2008)

- Tobacco dependence is a **chronic condition** that often requires repeated intervention.
- **Counselling and medication are each effective; combining them is more effective than either alone.**
- Seven first-line medications were identified as effective: five NRT forms (gum, patch, lozenge, inhaler, nasal spray), bupropion SR and varenicline.
- Clinicians should use the 5 A's model: Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange follow-up.
- Quitlines (e.g., 1-800-QUIT-NOW in the US) are effective and should be promoted.

## Status today

The 2008 guideline is the classic US reference but predates: the EAGLES safety trial (2016), cytisine trials, the e-cigarette evidence base and the 2020 Surgeon General report. It remains cited here because its central findings — dependence is chronic, treatment works, combination beats monotherapy — remain the foundation of every later guideline. For current US recommendations see [USPSTF 2021](uspstf-2021.md).


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/guidelines/uspstf-2021.md -->

# USPSTF 2021 — Interventions for Tobacco Smoking Cessation in Adults, Including Pregnant Persons

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Issuing body | U.S. Preventive Services Task Force |
| Year | 2021 |
| Publication | JAMA 2021;325(3):265-279 |
| DOI | [10.1001/jama.2020.25019](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2020.25019) |
| PMID | 33464343 |

## Recommendations

- **Nonpregnant adults (A recommendation)**: clinicians should ask all adults about tobacco use, advise stopping, and provide behavioural interventions and FDA-approved pharmacotherapy.
- **Pregnant persons (A recommendation)**: clinicians should ask about tobacco use, advise stopping, and provide behavioural interventions.
- **Pharmacotherapy in pregnancy (I statement)**: evidence insufficient to assess balance of benefits and harms.
- **E-cigarettes (I statement)**: evidence insufficient to assess benefits and harms for cessation in adults; clinicians should direct patients to interventions with proven effectiveness.

## Interpretation

The USPSTF position is the reference US preventive-care statement. Its A-grade recommendations mean high certainty of substantial net benefit. The two I statements mark genuine evidence gaps — not "no benefit", but "not yet proven" — which is why this site keeps e-cigarettes in the Controversies section rather than in Methods.


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/guidelines/who-2024.md -->

# WHO clinical treatment guideline for tobacco cessation in adults (2024)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Issuing body | World Health Organization (WHO) |
| Year | 2024 (first-ever WHO clinical guideline on tobacco cessation) |
| Scope | Adults using any tobacco product: cigarettes, waterpipes, smokeless tobacco, cigars, roll-your-own, heated tobacco products |
| Basis | GRADE evidence reviews |
| Source | [WHO publication 9789240096431](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240096431) |

## Key recommendations

- **Behavioural support**: brief advice (30 seconds to 3 minutes) should be offered to every tobacco user in health settings; more intensive individual, group or telephone counselling should be offered where feasible.
- **Digital interventions**: digital cessation interventions can be offered as complements to other support.
- **Pharmacotherapy (adults)**: recommends **varenicline, nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), bupropion and cytisine** as effective cessation medications. Choice should consider the user's medical context, preferences and availability.
- **Combination**: behavioural plus pharmacological treatment is recommended over either alone.
- **Smokeless tobacco**: specific recommendations for cessation of smokeless tobacco products are included.

## Notable context

- The guideline is written for health-care providers and for health-system managers; it is designed to be implementable in low-resource settings.
- WHO notes that in 2023 it initiated a prequalification procedure for cessation medications, and that NRT products were first prequalified in April 2024.
- On e-cigarettes: WHO states the current evidence is insufficient to recommend them as cessation aids at population level, while acknowledging that individual countries regulate them differently.

## Differences from other guidelines

Compared with NICE NG209 (UK), WHO is more cautious about e-cigarettes as cessation aids. Compared with USPSTF 2021, WHO explicitly includes cytisine, which is not FDA-approved in the US. All three agree on the core: offer behavioural support plus pharmacotherapy.


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/health-effects/index.md -->

# Health Effects: What Smoking Does and What Quitting Changes

The evidence layer on harm and recovery. The body-recovery timeline on the [main site](https://smokingcessationhub.com/timeline/) is the practical version of this page.

## The core evidence

- Smoking is causally linked to cancer, cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease, and many other conditions — the causal framework is documented across Surgeon General reports and WHO reports spanning decades.
- The landmark Jha et al. study of ~200,000 US adults found: quitting before age 40 avoids most of the excess mortality of continued smoking; quitting between 25–34 adds roughly a decade of life; quitting at any age confers benefit — see [R-006](../research/records/r-006.md).

## What happens after quitting (documented averages)

| Timeframe | Documented change |
|---|---|
| 20 min | Heart rate and blood pressure begin to drop |
| 12–24 h | Carbon monoxide clears from blood |
| Weeks | Circulation and lung function improve; coughing may transiently increase as cilia recover |
| 1–9 months | Cilia function recovers; cough and shortness of breath typically decrease |
| 1 year | Excess coronary heart disease risk roughly halves |
| 5 years | Stroke risk approaches that of a non-smoker |
| 10+ years | Lung cancer risk falls substantially; risks keep declining |

*These are population averages summarized from US Surgeon General and WHO materials; individual outcomes vary.*

## What the community reports

Community experiences in the database frequently describe easier breathing within weeks, taste and smell returning within days, and energy improvements over months. These reports are **consistent with** the evidence — they are not themselves evidence, and individual absence of noticeable benefit does not mean absence of biological recovery.

## What does NOT happen

- No health effect appears instantly reversible at the moment of the last cigarette.
- Quitting does not erase all accumulated risk; it substantially reduces future additional risk.
- Harm reduction products (e-cigarettes) are covered under [Controversies](../controversies/) — long-term safety is genuinely uncertain.

## Related

- [Research records R-006, R-007](../research/)
- [Withdrawal section](../withdrawal/) — the uncomfortable-but-temporary first weeks


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/index.md -->

# Quit Smoking Hub — Data Center

The evidence and knowledge infrastructure behind [Quit Smoking Hub](https://smokingcessationhub.com/). Where the main site gives practical knowledge, questions and community experiences, this site provides the structured evidence layer: research records, guidelines, definitions, evidence pages and the community data documentation.

## What this site is

- **Evidence layer**: every research record is a published, citable study — never invented, never summarized from memory. See [Research](research/).
- **Guideline comparison**: what WHO, USPSTF, NICE and the US PHS actually recommend, with dates and differences stated. See [Guidelines](guidelines/).
- **Medication and method evidence**: per-medication and per-method evidence pages with strength ratings. See [Medications](medications/) and [Cessation Methods](cessation-methods/).
- **Withdrawal science**: symptom-by-symptom science — definition, mechanism, timing, what varies, what may help. See [Withdrawal](withdrawal/).
- **Defined vocabulary**: a stable glossary used consistently across both sites. See [Definitions](definitions/).
- **Controversies, stated plainly**: e-cigarettes, gradual-vs-abrupt, dual use, medication comparisons. See [Controversies](controversies/).
- **Community data documentation**: how the experience database is built, its statistics, and its limits. See [Community Data](community-data/).

## The relationship between the two sites

| Main site | Data center |
|---|---|
| Practical knowledge and guidance | Evidence and structured records |
| Questions with direct answers | Research and guidelines behind the answers |
| Community experiences and patterns | Community data documentation and statistics |
| Timeline, tools, triggers | Withdrawal science, behaviour-change mechanisms |

The main site links here for evidence; this site links back for practical application. Neither duplicates the other.

## Evidence integrity rules

1. **No fabricated studies, authors, DOIs, PMIDs, statistics or findings.** Every record traces to its published source, linked from the record page.
2. **Community experience is not medical evidence.** Community data are reported as observations with their own documentation, always separate from the evidence layer.
3. **Uncertainty is stated, not smoothed over.** Where evidence conflicts or is insufficient, it says so — see [Controversies](controversies/).
4. **No individual medical advice.** Medication pages describe what the evidence shows; they never prescribe.

## Start points

- [Research Database](research/) — 17 structured records
- [Guidelines](guidelines/) — 4 major guideline records
- [Community statistics](community-data/statistics.md) — live counts from the experience database
- [Medical disclaimer](https://smokingcessationhub.com/disclaimer/) (main site)


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/medications/bupropion.md -->

# Bupropion

## What it is

A prescription medication (bupropion SR; also marketed as an antidepressant under other brand names) used for smoking cessation. It is not nicotine-based.

## How it works

Its exact mechanism in cessation is not fully understood. It affects dopamine and noradrenaline pathways implicated in reward and withdrawal, and appears to reduce craving and withdrawal symptoms.

## What the evidence shows

- The Cochrane review of antidepressants for smoking cessation found bupropion approximately doubles quit rates versus placebo — see [R-003](../research/records/r-003.md).
- In EAGLES, bupropion showed no significant increase in moderate-to-severe neuropsychiatric adverse events versus placebo — see [R-015](../research/records/r-015.md).
- WHO (2024), USPSTF (2021) and NICE (NG209) all include bupropion among recommended options; it is often the choice when varenicline is unavailable or unsuitable.

## Common considerations

- Insomnia and dry mouth are commonly reported.
- Bupropion lowers seizure threshold; it is **not used** in people with seizure disorders, eating disorders with purging, or certain other conditions — suitability is a clinical decision.
- It can be combined with NRT in some protocols; ask about combined treatment.

## Questions to ask a healthcare professional

- Do any of my conditions or medications interact with bupropion?
- What should I do if sleep becomes difficult after starting?
- Is combining bupropion with NRT appropriate for me?

**Related:** [Varenicline](varenicline.md) · [NRT](nrt.md) · [Research record R-003](../research/records/r-003.md)


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/medications/cytisine.md -->

# Cytisine

## What it is

A plant-derived partial agonist at nicotinic receptors — pharmacologically a cousin of varenicline, but far older and far cheaper. It has been used for smoking cessation in Eastern Europe for decades; a modernized form (cytisinicline) is under development.

## How it works

Like varenicline, it partially activates nicotinic receptors, easing withdrawal while reducing the reward from smoking. Treatment courses are typically short — about 25 days with a tapering tablet schedule.

## What the evidence shows

- West et al. (NEJM 2011): cytisine significantly increased 12-month abstinence versus placebo (8.4% vs 2.4%) — see [R-016](../research/records/r-016.md).
- Walker et al. (NEJM 2014): at 1 month, cytisine outperformed NRT (40% vs 31%); by 6 months the difference narrowed (22% vs 15%) and was not statistically significant, at a fraction of NRT's cost — see [R-017](../research/records/r-017.md).
- Cochrane's partial-agonists review covers cytisine within its scope — see [R-002](../research/records/r-002.md).
- WHO (2024) recommends cytisine; NICE added cytisinicline recommendations in its 2025 review. Cytisine is **not FDA-approved** in the US, so USPSTF's US recommendation set does not include it.

## Common considerations

- Dry mouth and gastrointestinal symptoms are commonly reported; side effects are generally mild and self-limiting.
- Cost is the standout feature: cytisine courses cost a small fraction of varenicline or NRT in most markets, which is why WHO emphasizes it for global access.
- Availability is the main practical barrier in countries where it is not licensed.

## Questions to ask a healthcare professional or pharmacist

- Is cytisine available and licensed where I live?
- Does the short course fit my situation, or would a longer treatment be better?
- How does cytisine compare with varenicline for me?

**Related:** [Varenicline](varenicline.md) · [NRT](nrt.md) · [WHO 2024 guideline](../guidelines/who-2024.md)


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/medications/index.md -->

# Cessation Medications

Evidence pages for the medications with the strongest published evidence: nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), varenicline, bupropion and cytisine. Each page reports what the medication is, how it works, what trials and systematic reviews show, common considerations, and questions to ask a healthcare professional.

**This is medication information, not medical advice and not prescriptions.** Dosing, suitability and interactions are individual clinical decisions. Any medication can have side effects; none of these pages substitutes for discussion with a prescriber or pharmacist.

## Evidence strength overview

| Medication | Best evidence | Effect on quit rates vs placebo (approx.) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Varenicline | Cochrane review of partial agonists | Roughly 2.2–2.9x | Also supported by EAGLES safety trial |
| NRT (any form) | Cochrane NRT review | Roughly 1.5–1.7x | Many forms; combination of patch + fast-acting form is common |
| Bupropion | Cochrane antidepressant review | Roughly 1.6x | Not with seizure-risk conditions |
| Cytisine | Cochrane + NEJM trials | Roughly 1.7–3x vs placebo; similar to NRT in comparative trials | Very low cost; not available in all countries |

*Figures are approximate ranges from the systematic reviews listed; exact estimates depend on setting and outcome definition. See the Research Database records for precise findings.*

## Pages

- [Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT)](nrt.md)
- [Varenicline](varenicline.md)
- [Bupropion](bupropion.md)
- [Cytisine](cytisine.md)

- [Research records R-001…R-017](../research/) — the underlying systematic reviews and trials


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/medications/nrt.md -->

# Nicotine Replacement Therapy (NRT)

## What it is

NRT supplies nicotine without tobacco smoke, in controlled doses, through a patch, gum, lozenge, inhaler or nasal spray. The patch provides slow, steady delivery; gum and lozenge deliver faster, on-demand relief.

## How it works

It reduces withdrawal symptoms and cravings while the person breaks the behavioural habit of smoking. Because the dose is lower and delivered without the rapid nicotine spike of a cigarette, dependence is typically easier to step down.

## What the evidence shows

- The Cochrane review of NRT (Stead et al.) found NRT in any form increases quit rates by roughly 50–70% versus placebo — see [R-001](../research/records/r-001.md).
- In the EAGLES trial, the nicotine patch showed no increase in moderate-to-severe neuropsychiatric adverse events versus placebo — see [R-015](../research/records/r-015.md).
- WHO (2024), USPSTF (2021) and NICE (NG209) all recommend NRT; in the UK, combining a patch with a fast-acting form (gum or lozenge) is standard practice.

## Common considerations

- Local irritation (patch), jaw discomfort (gum), throat/mouth irritation (lozenge) are commonly reported and usually mild.
- Vivid dreams or disturbed sleep can occur with 24-hour patch use; many people remove the patch at night.
- NRT is widely available without prescription in many countries, which makes it the most accessible first-line option.

## Questions to ask a healthcare professional

- Which form or combination suits my smoking pattern?
- How long should I continue NRT, and how should I taper?
- Are there reasons NRT is less suitable for me (pregnancy, cardiovascular history, recent heart attack)?

**Related:** [Bupropion](bupropion.md) · [Cytisine](cytisine.md) · [Withdrawal science](../withdrawal/)


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/medications/varenicline.md -->

# Varenicline

## What it is

A prescription medication (marketed as Chantix/Champix) developed specifically for smoking cessation. It is a partial agonist at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.

## How it works

It binds to the same brain receptors as nicotine. It partially stimulates them — reducing withdrawal and craving — while blocking nicotine from fully activating them, which reduces the reward of smoking.

## What the evidence shows

- Cochrane's review of nicotine receptor partial agonists found varenicline increases quit rates substantially versus placebo (roughly 2–3x) — see [R-002](../research/records/r-002.md).
- The EAGLES trial (8,144 participants, with and without psychiatric disorders) found **no significant increase in moderate-to-severe neuropsychiatric adverse events** versus placebo or patch, and varenicline was the most effective of the compared treatments — see [R-015](../research/records/r-015.md).
- The 2016 network meta-analysis overview placed varenicline among the most effective single medications — see [R-008](../research/records/r-008.md).
- WHO (2024), USPSTF (2021) and NICE (NG209) all recommend varenicline.

## Common considerations

- Nausea is the most commonly reported side effect, usually mild and early in treatment.
- Abnormal dreams and insomnia are also commonly reported.
- Following the EAGLES results, regulators removed the black-box neuropsychiatric warning. People with a history of psychiatric illness were included in the trial; individual assessment still matters.
- Availability varies by country and by supply history; generic forms exist in several markets.

## Questions to ask a healthcare professional

- Is varenicline suitable given my medical history and current medications?
- What should I expect in the first weeks, and what side effects should I report?
- How does it compare with NRT or cytisine for me specifically?

**Related:** [NRT](nrt.md) · [Bupropion](bupropion.md) · [EAGLES record](../research/records/r-015.md)


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/nicotine/index.md -->

# Nicotine: What It Is and How Dependence Works

Understanding nicotine is the foundation of understanding quitting. This page covers the pharmacology — what nicotine does in the brain, why dependence develops, and why withdrawal happens.

## What nicotine is

Nicotine is the primary addictive substance in tobacco. It is a stimulant alkaloid that reaches the brain within seconds when inhaled in cigarette smoke — faster than intravenous administration.

## How dependence develops

- Nicotine binds to **nicotinic acetylcholine receptors**, releasing dopamine in reward pathways. The fast spike and rapid clearance of cigarette-delivered nicotine makes the reinforcement loop unusually strong.
- With repeated use, the brain **adapts**: receptor numbers change, and normal function comes to depend on nicotine. This is neuroadaptation — the biological core of dependence.
- Behavioural conditioning then layers on top: lighting up becomes paired with coffee, driving, stress, alcohol, work breaks. The habit network is what keeps triggering urges long after the biology settles.

## Why withdrawal happens

When nicotine is removed, the adapted brain is temporarily out of balance. The mismatch between a brain "expecting" nicotine and not receiving it produces the withdrawal syndrome: irritability, craving, low mood, difficulty concentrating, sleep disturbance, increased appetite.

- Most physical withdrawal symptoms **peak in the first week and substantially resolve within 2–4 weeks** — see the Hughes withdrawal time-course record [R-007](../research/records/r-007.md).
- **Craving** behaves differently: it can persist for months, in waves, especially when conditioned triggers are encountered.

## Key distinction: dependence vs habit

| | Dependence | Conditioned habit |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Neuroadaptation requiring nicotine | Learned associations triggering urge |
| Timescale | Resolves over weeks | Weakens over months–years, by repetition |
| Treated by | NRT, varenicline, bupropion, cytisine | Behavioural change, trigger management |

Both matter, and they are treated differently — which is why combined medication + behavioural support outperforms either alone.

## Related

- [Withdrawal section](../withdrawal/) — symptom-by-symptom science
- [Definitions](../definitions/) — precise terms used across the platform
- [Main site: How to Quit Smoking](https://smokingcessationhub.com/quit-smoking/)

## Sourcing policy

- All DOIs above are real and link to the published record.
- Community experience data (experience database, relapse reports, patterns) are attributed to the de-identified ingestion pipeline described in the [main-site methodology](https://smokingcessationhub.com/methodology/) — they are not part of the scientific evidence base and are never cited as such.
- Sources are re-verified against the publisher when records are updated; each research record carries a last-verified date.


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/relapse/index.md -->

# Relapse: The Science of Returning to Smoking

## Definitions first

- **Lapse**: a single slip — one cigarette or a brief episode of smoking.
- **Relapse**: return to regular, ongoing smoking.
- **Abstinence**: sustained non-smoking over a defined period.

Conflating lapse with relapse is a common and harmful error: it turns a single cigarette into psychological defeat, when the evidence-based response to a lapse is recommitment, not surrender.

## What the evidence says about relapse risk

- Relapse is most likely in the **first weeks**; risk declines steeply after the first months and continues to decline over years. Long-term quitters still occasionally relapse, but the base rate falls sharply.
- **Lapses are common.** Many people who ultimately succeed long-term report one or more slips in their quit history — a pattern visible in the [community relapse reports](https://smokingcessationhub.com/relapse/) and consistent with the chronic-disease model of dependence (US PHS 2008).
- **Each quit attempt is informative**: attempts are learning data, not moral tests. Multiple attempts are the norm — see the community question on [attempt counts](https://smokingcessationhub.com/questions/).

## Documented relapse contexts (from community data)

The structured experience database documents recurring relapse contexts: alcohol and social occasions, post-lapse escalation back to full smoking, and the "just one cigarette" sequence. These are reported patterns, presented as observations — [patterns section on the main site](https://smokingcessationhub.com/patterns/).

## What helps after a lapse (evidence-informed)

1. **Do not extend the lapse** — the single strongest predictor of full relapse is continued smoking after a slip.
2. **Analyze the trigger** concretely: what cue, what time, who, what emotion.
3. **Write an if-then plan** for that specific situation next time.
4. **Consider whether treatment was sufficient** — unmedicated quits relapse more in trial data; discuss intensification (medication + support) if lapses recur.
5. **Restart immediately** if a full relapse occurs — a new attempt is not a new identity, it is the same process with more information.

## What NOT to infer

- A lapse does not mean the person "cannot quit".
- Community relapse stories are reports, not predictions of any individual's outcome.
- Relapse is not caused by a single factor — it is a convergence of trigger, opportunity, biology and moment.

## Related

- [Behaviour change section](../behavior-change/) — cue-routine-reward mechanics
- [Community relapse reports](https://smokingcessationhub.com/relapse/) (main site)
- [Withdrawal section](../withdrawal/) — the high-risk first weeks


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/research/index.md -->

# Research Database

Structured records of smoking cessation research. Every record captures the same core fields — title, authors, year, journal, DOI/PMID (when available), research type, population, intervention, comparator, main question, findings, limitations, evidence strength, relevance and a last-verified date.

**Sourcing rule:** records are created only from published, citable sources (journals, Cochrane, WHO, national agencies). No record, statistic or DOI on this site is invented. If a field was not available in the source, it is marked *Not reported*.

## Evidence hierarchy used across this platform

| Level | Source type | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Systematic review / meta-analysis of RCTs | Cochrane reviews |
| 2 | Randomized controlled trial | EAGLES, Hajek 2019 |
| 3 | Cohort / observational study | Jha 2013 |
| 4 | Clinical guideline (GRADE-based) | WHO 2024, USPHS |
| 5 | Government / public-health source | Surgeon General reports |
| 6 | Community experience | Quit Smoking Hub experience database |

Levels 1–5 are scientific evidence. Level 6 (community experience) is **not** medical evidence and is never presented as such.

# R-001: Nicotine replacement therapy for smoking cessation

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Research ID | R-001 |
| Authors | Stead LF, Perera R, Bullen C, et al. |
| Year | 2012 |
| Journal / publisher | Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |
| DOI | [10.1002/14651858.CD000146.pub4](https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD000146.pub4) |
| PMID | Not reported |
| ISBN | Not reported |
| Research type | Systematic Review |
| Evidence strength | Strong |
| Population | Not reported |
| Intervention | Not reported |
| Comparator | Not reported |
| Last verified | 2026-10-04 |

## Main question

Does nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) help people quit smoking?

## Main findings

NRT in any form (gum, patch, lozenge, inhaler, spray) increases the rate of quitting by roughly 50% to 70% compared with placebo or no medication, regardless of the setting.

## Limitations

Absolute quit rates remain modest; most participants do not succeed even with NRT.

## Why this record matters

Not reported

## Related topics

Nicotine Replacement Therapy; Quit Methods; Quit Smoking Medications

[https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD000146.pub4/full](https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD000146.pub4/full)

# R-003: Antidepressants for smoking cessation

## Main question

Do antidepressants, particularly bupropion, help people quit smoking?

## Main findings

Bupropion roughly doubles quit rates compared with placebo and is effective regardless of depression history. Nortriptyline also helps; other antidepressants show less evidence.

Bupropion is less effective than varenicline and combination NRT in indirect comparisons; contraindications apply.

# R-005: A randomized trial of e-cigarettes versus nicotine-replacement therapy

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Research ID | R-005 |
| Authors | Hajek P, Phillips-Waller A, Przulj D, et al. |
| Year | 2019 |
| Journal / publisher | New England Journal of Medicine |

| Population | 886 UK adults attending stop-smoking services |
| Intervention | Not reported |
| Comparator | Not reported |
| Last verified | 2026-10-04 |

## Main question

Are nicotine e-cigarettes more effective than conventional NRT for quitting smoking?

## Main findings

One-year abstinence was 18.0% in the e-cigarette group versus 9.9% in the NRT group. E-cigarette users reported less severe urges and more throat/mouth irritation.

## Limitations

Products and setting (UK stop-smoking service with behavioral support) may limit generalizability; long-term safety remains open.

# R-006: 21st-century hazards of smoking and benefits of cessation in the United States

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Research ID | R-006 |
| Authors | Jha P, Ramasundarahettige C, Landsman V, et al. |
| Year | 2013 |
| Journal / publisher | New England Journal of Medicine |
| DOI | [10.1056/NEJMsa1211128](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMsa1211128) |
| PMID | Not reported |
| ISBN | Not reported |
| Research type | Cohort Study |
| Evidence strength | Strong |
| Population | ~200,000 US adults followed over time |
| Intervention | Not reported |
| Comparator | Not reported |
| Last verified | 2026-10-04 |

## Main question

What are the mortality risks of continued smoking, and what are the benefits of quitting at different ages?

## Main findings

Smokers lose about a decade of life on average. Quitting before age 40 avoids roughly 90% of the excess risk; quitting at 50–59 avoids a substantial share, with benefits at every age.

## Limitations

Observational design; smoking behavior self-reported at baseline.

## Why this record matters

Not reported

## Related topics

# R-007: Effects of abstinence from tobacco: valid symptoms and time course

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Research ID | R-007 |
| Authors | Hughes JR |
| Year | 2007 |
| Journal / publisher | Nicotine & Tobacco Research |

| Intervention | Not reported |

| Last verified | 2026-10-04 |

## Main question

Which withdrawal symptoms are valid and how long do they last?

## Main findings

Valid withdrawal symptoms include craving, irritability, restlessness, difficulty concentrating, depressed mood, insomnia, and increased appetite. Most symptoms peak in the first week and resolve within 2–4 weeks; craving and increased appetite can persist longer.

## Limitations

Derived largely from clinical trial data; individual variation is substantial.

## Why this record matters

Not reported

## Related topics

Nicotine Withdrawal; Quit Timeline; Cravings

# R-013: Electronic cigarettes for smoking cessation (living systematic review, 2024 update)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Research ID | R-013 |
| Authors | Lindson N, Butler AR, McRobbie H, Bullen C, Hajek P, Begh R, Theodoulou A, Notley C, Rigotti NA, Turner T, Livingstone-Banks J, Morris T, Hartmann-Boyce J |
| Year | 2024 |
| Journal / publisher | Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |
| DOI | [10.1002/14651858.CD010216.pub8](https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD010216.pub8) |

| ISBN | Not reported |

| Evidence strength | Strong |

# R-017: Cytisine versus nicotine for smoking cessation

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Research ID | R-017 |
| Authors | Walker N, Howe C, Glover M, et al. |
| Year | 2014 |
| Journal / publisher | New England Journal of Medicine |
| DOI | [10.1056/NEJMoa1407764](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1407764) |
| PMID | Not reported |
| ISBN | Not reported |
| Research type | Randomized Controlled Trial (open-label, noninferiority) |

| Intervention | Cytisine 25-day course |

| Last verified | 2026-10-04 |

At 1 month, continuous abstinence was higher with cytisine (40% vs 31%); at 6 months the difference narrowed (22% vs 15%) and was not statistically significant. Cytisine was far cheaper than NRT.
