<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/withdrawal/anxiety.md -->

# Anxiety — Withdrawal Science

## Definition

Feelings of tension, worry, nervousness or panic-like symptoms during the withdrawal period.

## Why it happens

Nicotine withdrawal dysregulates the stress-response systems that nicotine chronically activated; quitting also removes a coping behaviour people often used to manage stress, temporarily unmasking anxiety.

## Typical timing

Typically emerges in the first days, peaks in week 1, and settles over 2–4 weeks for most people.

## What research says

Anxiety is documented as a withdrawal symptom (see R-007), though the effect size varies across studies. People with anxiety disorders may notice a more pronounced response early in quitting.

## What varies between people

Wide variation: many people report calmness and relief rather than anxiety; others report notable tension. Baseline anxiety matters — someone quitting with an untreated anxiety disorder may need extra support.

## What may help

Slow breathing exercises, reducing caffeine, physical activity, structured relaxation, and planned responses to worry spirals. Behavioural support can help distinguish withdrawal anxiety from underlying anxiety.

## When medical advice may be appropriate

Seek professional help for panic attacks, persistent severe anxiety lasting beyond the withdrawal window, or if anxiety prevents normal functioning.

---
*Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see [R-007](../research/records/r-007.md)) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the [main site withdrawal section](https://smokingcessationhub.com/withdrawal/).*


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/withdrawal/appetite-weight.md -->

# Increased Appetite and Weight Change — Withdrawal Science

## Definition

Greater hunger, snacking, taste improvement and weight gain after quitting.

## Why it happens

Nicotine suppresses appetite and slightly raises metabolism; withdrawal reverses both. Food also substitutes for the oral habit, and taste/smell recovery makes food more rewarding. Weight gain is typically modest.

## Typical timing

Appetite rises in the first weeks; weight gain typically occurs over the first months, with most of it in the first 3–6 months.

## What research says

Average weight gain after quitting is commonly cited as about 4–5 kg over the first year in population studies, with wide variation — many people gain less, some more. Increased appetite is documented in R-007.

## What varies between people

Highly variable: some people gain no weight; heavy smokers gain more on average. Fear of weight gain is a documented barrier to quitting for some groups.

## What may help

Planning snacks (fruit, vegetables, water), keeping hands busy, building in physical activity from day one, and accepting modest weight change as vastly less harmful than continued smoking.

## When medical advice may be appropriate

Rapid large weight gain or disordered eating patterns deserve professional attention; also note bupropion is sometimes discussed in this context — talk to a clinician.

---
*Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see [R-007](../research/records/r-007.md)) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the [main site withdrawal section](https://smokingcessationhub.com/withdrawal/).*


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/withdrawal/concentration.md -->

# Concentration Problems — Withdrawal Science

## Definition

Difficulty focusing, foggy thinking and slower mental processing during early withdrawal.

## Why it happens

Nicotine acutely enhances attention, and the adapted brain performs worse when nicotine is removed — until it re-adapts. Sleep disruption compounds the effect.

## Typical timing

Begins within days, peaks in week 1–2, and generally resolves within 2–4 weeks.

## What research says

Difficulty concentrating is one of the most reliably documented withdrawal symptoms (see R-007).

## What varies between people

Office workers report this as one of the most disruptive symptoms; physical laborers often notice it less. People who used cigarettes as a focus ritual lose that cue too.

## What may help

Breaking work into short blocks, writing lists, reducing multitasking expectations for the first weeks, staying hydrated, and protecting sleep. Remind yourself it is temporary — cognition returns to baseline.

## When medical advice may be appropriate

If concentration problems persist long after the withdrawal window or interfere severely, discuss with a professional — they can also reflect sleep or mood conditions.

---
*Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see [R-007](../research/records/r-007.md)) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the [main site withdrawal section](https://smokingcessationhub.com/withdrawal/).*


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/withdrawal/constipation.md -->

# Constipation — Withdrawal Science

## Definition

Less frequent or harder bowel movements in the first weeks after quitting.

## Why it happens

Nicotine stimulates bowel motility; its removal slows the gut temporarily. This is the inverse of the appetite increase — both reflect the gut adjusting to life without nicotine.

## Typical timing

Typically appears in week 1–2 and resolves within 2–4 weeks.

## What research says

Constipation is a recognized but less-studied withdrawal symptom (see R-007); gut effects are well known clinically.

## What varies between people

People with pre-existing slow gut habits or low fiber intake notice it most; many people never experience it.

## What may help

Water, dietary fiber, physical movement, and not ignoring the urge. Temporary use of standard fiber supplements or mild laxatives as directed is common practice.

## When medical advice may be appropriate

Constipation with severe pain, blood in stool, or lasting more than a few weeks warrants medical evaluation.

---
*Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see [R-007](../research/records/r-007.md)) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the [main site withdrawal section](https://smokingcessationhub.com/withdrawal/).*


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/withdrawal/cough.md -->

# Cough — Withdrawal Science

## Definition

Increased coughing and phlegm production in the weeks after quitting — often called the 'quitter's cough'.

## Why it happens

Tobacco smoke paralyzes the cilia that clean the airways. When smoke exposure stops, cilia recover and begin clearing accumulated mucus — the cough is the clean-out process, not damage.

## Typical timing

Often appears or worsens in weeks 1–4 after quitting, then improves as airways clear; some people cough for a few months.

## What research says

The temporal cough increase after cessation is well described clinically; lung function improvements after quitting are documented in the Surgeon General's reports.

## What varies between people

Some people never notice it; long-term heavy smokers notice it most. The cough should progressively improve — a cough that keeps worsening beyond months needs evaluation.

## What may help

Hydration, humidified air, and patience — it is a sign of recovery. Persistent or severe cough is not helped by resuming smoking, which restarts the damage.

## When medical advice may be appropriate

Cough with blood, persistent fever, chest pain, or a cough that worsens progressively for more than a few weeks warrants prompt medical evaluation.

---
*Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see [R-007](../research/records/r-007.md)) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the [main site withdrawal section](https://smokingcessationhub.com/withdrawal/).*


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/withdrawal/cravings.md -->

# Craving — Withdrawal Science

## Definition

An intense urge or desire to smoke — the core symptom of nicotine dependence.

## Why it happens

Craving has two sources: the nicotine-adapted brain signalling for nicotine (pharmacological craving), and conditioned triggers (coffee, alcohol, stress, places, routines) activating learned associations. The second source is why cravings return long after physical dependence resolves.

## Typical timing

Cravings begin within hours of the last cigarette, peak in the first days, and occur in waves. Frequency and intensity decline over weeks, but individual cravings can still appear months later, usually when a conditioned trigger is encountered.

## What research says

Cravings are the most persistent withdrawal symptom; the Hughes review documents that unlike most other symptoms they do not fully resolve within 2–4 weeks (see R-007). Conditioned-cue craving is well documented in cue-reactivity research.

## What varies between people

People differ sharply: some report near-constant early craving, others report brief passing urges. Craving intensity correlates with dependence level but individual conditioning (rituals, places, people) matters more than dose.

## What may help

Distraction, delay, drinking water, deep breathing, physical movement, and pre-planned responses to known triggers. Fast-acting NRT (gum, lozenge) targets the pharmacological component; trigger management targets the conditioned component.

## When medical advice may be appropriate

Cravings alone are not a medical concern, but if accompanied by chest pain, severe dizziness or symptoms suggesting another condition, seek evaluation.

---
*Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see [R-007](../research/records/r-007.md)) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the [main site withdrawal section](https://smokingcessationhub.com/withdrawal/).*


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/withdrawal/fatigue.md -->

# Fatigue — Withdrawal Science

## Definition

Unusual tiredness, low energy or heavy sleepiness in early withdrawal.

## Why it happens

Nicotine is a stimulant; withdrawal removes a chronic activation source. Sleep disruption, stress and the energy cost of brain re-adaptation all contribute.

## Typical timing

Common in the first 1–2 weeks, improving over 2–4 weeks.

## What research says

Fatigue is documented in withdrawal symptom research, though it overlaps with sleep and mood symptoms (see R-007).

## What varies between people

Some people feel energized immediately; others feel drained. People quitting with anemia, thyroid conditions or poor sleep report more fatigue.

## What may help

Prioritizing sleep, short walks (mild activity paradoxically reduces fatigue), regular meals, and temporarily reducing commitments in the first weeks.

## When medical advice may be appropriate

Fatigue persisting well beyond the withdrawal window, or accompanied by breathlessness, pallor, weight loss or night sweats, needs medical review.

---
*Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see [R-007](../research/records/r-007.md)) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the [main site withdrawal section](https://smokingcessationhub.com/withdrawal/).*


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/withdrawal/headache.md -->

# Headache — Withdrawal Science

## Definition

Headaches in the first weeks after quitting, ranging from mild tension-type to more noticeable episodes.

## Why it happens

Multiple mechanisms: blood flow changes as nicotine's vascular effects withdraw, caffeine-nicotine interaction changes, sleep disruption, and general stress. Nicotine is a vasoconstrictor; withdrawal changes cerebral circulation.

## Typical timing

Usually within the first days to week, resolving over 1–3 weeks.

## What research says

Headache is a documented though less consistently reported withdrawal symptom (see R-007).

## What varies between people

Caffeine users who change coffee intake while quitting often trigger headaches — nicotine speeds caffeine metabolism, so the same coffee is effectively stronger after quitting.

## What may help

Regular hydration, stable sleep, watching caffeine intake (consider slightly reducing coffee in the first weeks), and standard over-the-counter pain relief used as directed.

## When medical advice may be appropriate

Sudden severe headache, headache with visual changes, weakness, confusion or stiff neck needs urgent medical evaluation — these are not withdrawal.

---
*Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see [R-007](../research/records/r-007.md)) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the [main site withdrawal section](https://smokingcessationhub.com/withdrawal/).*


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/withdrawal/index.md -->

# Withdrawal: The Science

Withdrawal is the body and brain readjusting after nicotine is removed. This section covers each major symptom: what it is, why it happens, typical timing and duration, what research documents, what varies between people, and what may help.

## The core evidence

The time-course is documented by the landmark Hughes review — see [R-007](../research/records/r-007.md):

- Most physical symptoms **peak in the first week** and substantially resolve within **2–4 weeks**.
- **Craving** is the exception — it declines slowly and can persist for months in waves.
- Symptoms vary widely between individuals in both intensity and duration.

## Symptom overview

| Symptom | Typical onset | Typical duration | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| Craving | Immediate | Weeks–months, in waves | [cravings](cravings.md) |
| Irritability | Day 1–3 | Peaks week 1, resolves ~2–4 weeks | [irritability](irritability.md) |
| Anxiety | Day 1–3 | Usually 2–4 weeks | [anxiety](anxiety.md) |
| Low mood | Day 1–3 | Usually 2–4 weeks | [low-mood](low-mood.md) |
| Sleep problems | Day 1–7 | Usually 2–4 weeks | [sleep](sleep.md) |
| Concentration problems | Day 1–7 | Usually 2–4 weeks | [concentration](concentration.md) |
| Restlessness | Day 1–7 | Usually 2–4 weeks | [restlessness](restlessness.md) |
| Increased appetite / weight change | Week 1+ | Months for weight | [appetite-weight](appetite-weight.md) |
| Cough | Week 1+ | Weeks–months (may transiently worsen) | [cough](cough.md) |
| Headache | Day 1–7 | Usually 1–3 weeks | [headache](headache.md) |
| Fatigue | Day 1–7 | Usually 2–4 weeks | [fatigue](fatigue.md) |
| Constipation | Week 1+ | Usually 2–4 weeks | [constipation](constipation.md) |

*Timings are typical patterns from the research literature and clinical descriptions, not guarantees — individual variation is the rule.*

## Important boundary

Withdrawal symptoms are usually mild-to-moderate and self-limiting. Some symptoms — chest pain, blood-streaked phlegm, persistent fever, severe or worsening breathlessness — are **not typical withdrawal** and warrant medical evaluation. The practical, plain-language version lives on the [main site](https://smokingcessationhub.com/withdrawal/).


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/withdrawal/irritability.md -->

# Irritability — Withdrawal Science

## Definition

Lower frustration tolerance, short temper, anger and general edginess in the first weeks after quitting.

## Why it happens

The nicotine-adapted brain temporarily loses the calming effect of repeated nicotine dosing; combined with sleep disruption and the stress of breaking a habit, frustration tolerance drops.

## Typical timing

Appears within 1–3 days, peaks in the first week, and typically resolves within 2–4 weeks.

## What research says

Irritability/anger is one of the most consistently documented withdrawal symptoms in the literature (see R-007). It is rated among the most severe symptoms by people quitting.

## What varies between people

Severity ranges from mild edginess to notable anger episodes. People with pre-existing stress or mood conditions may experience more pronounced irritability.

## What may help

Warning family and colleagues, scheduled physical activity, adequate sleep, reducing caffeine late in the day, and giving yourself permission to step away from tense situations.

## When medical advice may be appropriate

If anger becomes uncontrollable, or is accompanied by severe mood disturbance or thoughts of self-harm, seek professional help — that is beyond typical withdrawal.

---
*Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see [R-007](../research/records/r-007.md)) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the [main site withdrawal section](https://smokingcessationhub.com/withdrawal/).*


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/withdrawal/low-mood.md -->

# Low Mood — Withdrawal Science

## Definition

Sadness, low energy of mood, reduced interest or mild depressive feelings during withdrawal.

## Why it happens

Removing nicotine disrupts dopamine signalling that cigarettes chronically stimulated; the brain needs time to re-regulate. Loss of a daily ritual and its social rewards also contributes.

## Typical timing

Usually begins in the first days, is most noticeable in weeks 1–2, and improves by ~4 weeks.

## What research says

Depressed mood is a documented withdrawal symptom (see R-007). It is distinct from clinical depression: withdrawal low mood is time-limited and resolves as neuroadaptation reverses.

## What varies between people

People with a history of depression are at higher risk of a more pronounced low mood, and it can be hard to tell withdrawal low mood from emerging depressive relapse — an important reason to involve a professional early.

## What may help

Maintaining routines, physical activity (with the strongest evidence for mood), social contact, realistic expectations about the first weeks, and planning pleasant activities deliberately.

## When medical advice may be appropriate

If low mood persists beyond a month, deepens, or includes hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm, seek professional evaluation promptly. This is a safety boundary, not a weakness.

---
*Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see [R-007](../research/records/r-007.md)) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the [main site withdrawal section](https://smokingcessationhub.com/withdrawal/).*


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/withdrawal/restlessness.md -->

# Restlessness — Withdrawal Science

## Definition

An inability to sit still, fidgeting, pacing, or a constant sense of needing to do something with the hands.

## Why it happens

Nicotine withdrawal produces psychomotor agitation; the smoking ritual also occupied the hands and filled micro-breaks, and removing it leaves a physical void.

## Typical timing

Early and prominent in the first week, fading over 2–4 weeks.

## What research says

Restlessness is among the consistently measured withdrawal symptoms (see R-007).

## What varies between people

People with strong hand-mouth rituals (smoking while working, driving, phoning) report more restlessness. Activity level also matters — moving people are less bothered.

## What may help

Fidget substitutes (pens, stress balls), short walks, standing breaks, chewing sugar-free gum, and keeping hands busy during formerly-smoking activities.

## When medical advice may be appropriate

Not usually a medical concern; if accompanied by chest pain, palpitations or tremor, seek evaluation.

---
*Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see [R-007](../research/records/r-007.md)) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the [main site withdrawal section](https://smokingcessationhub.com/withdrawal/).*


<!-- https://data.smokingcessationhub.com/llms/withdrawal/sleep.md -->

# Sleep Problems — Withdrawal Science

## Definition

Insomnia, frequent waking, vivid dreams or daytime sleepiness in the weeks after quitting.

## Why it happens

Nicotine is a stimulant and its withdrawal changes sleep architecture; nicotine also suppresses REM sleep, and quitting produces a rebound of vivid dreaming as REM normalizes.

## Typical timing

Sleep disturbance typically starts in the first days, peaks in week 1, and improves over 2–4 weeks. Vivid dreams can persist longer, especially with 24-hour nicotine patch use.

## What research says

Sleep disturbance and increased dreaming are documented withdrawal features (see R-007). Vivid dreams are also a known effect of nicotine patches worn overnight.

## What varies between people

Some people sleep better almost immediately (no more nocturnal nicotine cravings); others struggle for weeks. Patch users who sleep poorly often benefit from removing the patch at night.

## What may help

Consistent sleep schedule, reducing caffeine after midday, evening wind-down routines, and avoiding screens before bed. If using a 24-hour patch and dreams are disruptive, discuss patch timing with a pharmacist.

## When medical advice may be appropriate

Prolonged severe insomnia beyond the withdrawal window, or sleep apnea symptoms (loud snoring with pauses, daytime sleepiness), warrant medical review.

---
